entries.title: Bakahaza
entries.definitive_edition: Japanese Android mobile release, if legally preserved

emulation.notes: Use Android hardware or emulator only with a legally preserved build. iOS capture requires an owned app/account/device path.

primary.version: Japanese mobile release via preserved Android build
primary.why: No dedicated public release entry was found in this pass. BAKHAZA/BAKAHAZA is a Japanese iOS and Android mobile game, with iOS in 2016 and Android in 2017. For archive capture, Android is the practical primary route because a preserved build can be captured through Android hardware or emulator; no platform-exclusive content difference exists.
primary.how_to_play: Use a legally preserved Android build on real Android hardware or an Android emulator. If the Android build cannot be obtained, use the iOS release only if it is already tied to an account/device; do not substitute a fan recreation.

entries.remaster_caveats: No remaster or non-mobile port was found. No dedicated public release references game page was found during this pass.

entries.title: Resident Evil Code Veronica

emulation.notes: Prefer original HD console capture if emulation introduces rendering issues.

entries.remaster_caveats: The original Dreamcast release is historically important but not the most complete story cut.

entries.title: Resident Evil 4

emulation.notes: Use native PC. Dolphin is optional only for Wii control sampling.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: PC Ultimate HD with RE4 HD Project textures and tested 60 fps.

primary.version: Ultimate HD Edition + RE4 HD Project
primary.why: The PC Ultimate HD Edition contains the post-GameCube bonus content and, with the RE4 HD Project, has the strongest fidelity path for the 2005 game.
primary.how_to_play: Install the Windows Ultimate HD Edition, apply the RE4 HD Project, and use stable 60 fps settings only if the setup is tested before a full playthrough.

secondary.what_to_play: Interesting control style, but not required for Sami's content-first secondary rule.

entries.remaster_caveats: The 2023 remake is a different game and should be archived separately, not treated as the definitive version of the 2005 release.

entries.title: Resident Evil

emulation.notes: Use the documented primary route where possible; test any emulator or compatibility layer before a full archive run.

primary.version: Original PC release - modern GOG/Steam compatible build
primary.why: For the original 1996 game, Windows is the best primary because it has uncensored/color FMV and sharper PC graphics, with modern GOG/Steam compatibility now available. Saturn, Director's Cut, and Deadly Silence remain separate secondary/standalone routes for their exclusive modes.
primary.how_to_play: Play the modern Windows PC rerelease from GOG or Steam, then use the Saturn/Director's Cut/Deadly Silence entries only for their exclusive modes if desired.

secondary.what_to_play: Play the Battle Game and inspect Saturn-exclusive content only.
secondary.why: The Windows route is best for the main original campaign; Saturn has extra mode/content.

secondary.what_to_play: Use the dedicated Director's Cut entry for those modes.
secondary.why: Extra modes are not part of the Windows primary route.

secondary.what_to_play: Use the dedicated Deadly Silence entry for DS-exclusive modes.
secondary.why: DS mode content is separate from the PC primary route.

entries.remaster_caveats: This is the 1996 original, not the 2002 remake or HD Remaster; those have separate entries.

hdrWriteup.title: Why my HDR sliders look like that (and why yours might differ)
paragraphs: Resident Evil Requiem uses IN-GAME HDR - you calibrate it inside the game, not just in Windows. The catch: the in-game calibration image is misleading. The sliders show no numbers, and the picture you adjust against doesn't reflect what the game actually outputs, so it nudges you toward the wrong values on a bright display.

My monitor is an OLED that peaks around 1000 nits in HDR. Analysis of the game's actual output shows the Max Brightness slider reaches roughly 950 nits when pushed fully right (+20), while the default center (0) only puts out around 700 nits. So on a ~1000-nit screen I slide Max Brightness all the way right to use the full range my panel can show - the calibration image makes that look 'too bright,' but the real output is right where it should be.
Min Brightness goes fully left (-20) to hold a true black point. On an OLED, black pixels are genuinely off, so keeping the floor down preserves real inky blacks instead of lifting shadows into grey.

Brightness HDR I leave dead center at the default (0, about 300 nits). That's the mid/paper-white balance for the tone-map - the cleanest, easiest-on-the-eyes middle ground; pushing it just crushes or washes the mid-tones.

Important: these are tuned to MY 1000-nit OLED. If your monitor peaks lower (say 400-600 nits) you should NOT slam Max Brightness fully right - match it to your own panel's peak. Treat my numbers as the reference for a 1000-nit OLED, not a universal preset.

nvidia.title: driver control panel settings
nvidia.intro: These are my actual driver control panel settings, read straight off my screen - not defaults. I do most of the tuning at the global level so every game inherits it, and Resident Evil Requiem reads from that same global profile (no separate per-game overrides). Driver: GeForce Game Ready 610.62. The headline ones: Power Management on Prefer maximum performance, Texture Filtering on High quality, V-Sync On with G-SYNC, a 237 FPS frame cap, and the DLSS model-preset override below.

dlss.title: DLSS version swap (via DLSS Swapper)
dlss.intro: I updated all of Requiem's DLSS DLLs to the latest version using the DLSS Swapper app - upscaling, Ray Reconstruction, and Frame Generation - then set DLSS to Max Quality and Frame Generation to DLSS 4x in-game. The game shipped with the 310.3 DLLs; these are what I run now:
dlss.note: DLSS Swapper only changes the DLL version - it keeps a backup of the original (.dlsss) so you can revert. The actual quality preset (Max Quality) and frame-gen multiplier (4x) are set in the game's own menu, not in the swapper.

settings.settingsNote: Every setting above is read directly from the game's own config (config.ini, GameOption + render blocks), the NVIDIA driver profile database, and the DLSS Swapper database - so it matches exactly what runs on stream. Resident Evil Requiem keeps its audio levels, language, and subtitle settings inside the encrypted Steam Cloud save rather than the readable config file, so those few aren't listed here. Audio for the stream is handled on the mixer side (SM7B + RODECaster), not in-game.

mods.name: REFramework
mods.note: The modding framework for RE Engine games - required to load the script mods below. Installed here as dinput8.dll in the game folder.

mods.name: No Film Grain (REFramework script)
mods.note: Disables the film-grain filter at runtime for a clean, sharp picture on stream - on top of the in-game film grain already being off.

mods.name: Requiem FOV (REFramework script)
mods.note: Adds the field-of-view control the game ships without. Set wide but not fish-eye: 100 degrees horizontal for both Leon and Grace; aim-down-sights left at stock so it still zooms in. Per-character Leon/Grace profiles, and the interaction prompts and item markers stay anchored across the camera change.

settings.modsNote: Single-player, offline only. Every one of these is a PRESENTATION or capture adjustment - film grain, motion blur, lens distortion, vignette, field of view - never content, art, enemies, or difficulty. Same principle as running the game sharper than the hardware of its day could: the game the developers built is untouched; only how it reaches the camera changes. Installed with Vortex plus hand-placed REFramework scripts.
